text.p: In presenting a finding that could influence policies for saving diversity in the environment, a conservation group on Thursday said world lenders should focus on saving 17 "hotspots" worldwide.
Conservation International said that more than half of the world's land species are contained in less than 2 percent of its surface and the group released a map of biodiversity hotspots.
"This new map makes the biodiversity crisis much more manageable," Russell Mittermeier, Conservation International president said.

The map listed 17 priority areas, mostly in tropical climates, which it said contained more than 50 percent of the world's terrestrial biodiverisity, including high percentages of plants and vertebrates found only in those areas.
These hotspots should get special attention from conservationists and institutions such as the World Bank to save them as habitat, Mittermeier said at a briefing.
"What we're saying to potential donors is you can really come to grips with this by focusing a good portion of your attention on these hotspots," he said.

Already vast portions of these biological centres have been lost to development, Mittermeier said, and stressed that an approach of concentrating on hotspots did not mean nations should abandon efforts to save their own biological diversity.
"Every nation's biodiversity is critically important to its future, and must be the most fundamental component of any national strategy," he said.

Central and South American hotspots were the Tropical Andes of Venezuela, Colombia, Ecuador, Peru and Bolivia; the Atlantic forests of Brazil, Paraguay and Argentina; Brazil's Cerrado forests, western Ecuador, Panama's Darien and Colombia and Ecuador's Choco forests, the Antilles Islands, and the Meso-American Forests of Mexico and Central America.
African hotspots were the Guinean forests of West Africa, the Cape and Western Cape floristic region of South Africa, and the island of Madagascar.
Europe's hotspot was the Eastern Mediterranean region.
In Asia, hotspots were the Western Sunda region of Indonesia, Malaysia and Brunei; the Eastern Sunda region of Indonesia; the Philippines and the Western Ghats of India and the island of Sri Lanka.
Hotspots also included southwestern Australia, New Caledonia and the Polynesia and Micronesia Island complex including Hawaii and Fiji.

Conservation International said a list of second-tier biodiversity hotspots was being prepared that included the area from southern Oregon to the Baja Peninsula in the United States and the Caucasus Mountains of the former Soviet Union.
